chapter.title: A share is a slice of a shop

cards.body: A share's price can change several times a second, and most of those changes come from traders, not from the company. Think of the stock market as one huge organised bazaar: each company is a shop, and a share is a tiny slice of owning that shop. The price of a slice is just **whatever the last buyer and the last seller agreed on**, a moment ago.
cards.simpler: A share's price can change several times in one second, and most of those changes come from traders, not the company. Picture the stock market as one giant, busy bazaar. Each company is a shop, and a share is a tiny slice of owning that shop. The price of that slice is just **whatever the last buyer and the last seller agreed on**, a moment ago.

cards.prompt: Chandni Chowk, 11 am. People are trading slices of a famous jalebi shop. 40 people want to buy a slice, and only 4 owners want to sell. What happens to the price next?

options.text: It rises. Buyers compete, so sellers can ask for more.
It stays put, because the shop fixed it this morning.
It falls, because more people means more slices to go around.

whyNot.b: That's a menu price, not a share price: nobody fixes a share's price. It moves with every deal.
whyNot.c: That's mixing up buyers with slices: more buyers don't add slices. They fight over the same few.

cards.reteach: Many buyers and few sellers means the few sellers can ask for more. The price climbs until enough buyers give up and the two sides balance.

cards.title: What's in your hand
cards.body:
A company cuts its ownership into equal pieces called *shares*. Big Indian companies are cut into crores of pieces, so 1 share is like one grain from a full rice godown. It's tiny, but it's legally yours, with a sliver of the profits and a vote at the yearly meeting.

Here's the part people miss. After a company first sells its shares, it mostly steps back. From then on, you usually buy your slice from another owner who wants out, not from the company.

So the price isn't a tag the company sticks on. It's **the last deal between two strangers**, and the next deal can be a rupee higher or lower.
cards.simpler: A company splits its ownership into equal pieces called shares. Big Indian companies have crores of them, so one share is like one grain in a rice godown. Tiny, but legally yours, with a cut of profits and a vote each year. After the company's first sale, it mostly steps aside, and you usually buy from an owner who wants out. The price is **the last deal between two strangers**, and the next can be a rupee up or down.

cards.title: One minute in a share's life
cards.body: Say a paint company's share last traded at ₹500. At 10:02 am, 300 people want to buy at ₹500, but only 100 owners will sell at that price. The 200 left over start offering ₹501, then ₹502, then ₹503, and at each step a few owners who refused ₹500 say yes. The screen now shows ₹503, up 0.6%, and not one tin of paint changed in that minute.
cards.simpler: Say a paint company's share last sold for ₹500. At 10:02 am, 300 people want to buy at ₹500, but only 100 owners will sell at that price. The 200 left over start offering ₹501, then ₹502, then ₹503. At each step, a few owners who said no at ₹500 say yes. The screen now shows ₹503, up 0.6%, and **not one tin of paint changed** in that minute.

cards.prompt: A bank's share opens at ₹800 and closes at ₹776. Your cousin asks why. Which answer uses today's idea?

options.text: All day, sellers were keener to get out than buyers were to get in, so sellers kept taking lower prices.
The bank cut its share price by ₹24 this afternoon.
The bank lost ₹24 on every account today.

whyNot.b: That's a price tag, not a share price: the company doesn't set it. Strangers trading with each other do, one deal at a time.
whyNot.c: That's the bank's business, not its share price: the price fell because sellers were keener than buyers.

cards.reteach: Every rupee the price moved came from deals between buyers and sellers. A ₹24 fall means sellers kept agreeing to less, because there weren't enough buyers at the old price.

cards.title: Where headlines fit
cards.body:
You'd think news moves prices. It does, but only by changing how many people want to buy or sell. A headline is a stone thrown into the crowd at the stall. The price moves only if people move.

That's why good news can arrive with a falling price. If everyone expected great results and already bought, nobody is left to push the price higher. Then a few owners cash out.

Benjamin Graham, who taught Warren Buffett, built his whole approach on this gap: **price is what the crowd just paid, value is what the shop is actually worth**. They are often not the same number.
cards.simpler: News moves prices only by changing how many people want to buy or sell. A headline is a stone thrown into a crowd. Prices move only if people move. So good news can come with a falling price. If everyone already bought expecting great results, no buyers are left, and a few owners cash out. Warren Buffett's teacher Benjamin Graham built on this gap: **price is what the crowd just paid, value is what the shop is actually worth**.

cards.body: Priya reads "record profits" at 9:30 am, buys at 9:40, and watches the share fall 2% by lunch. She decides the market is rigged. What actually happened: the eager buyers had already bought last week, and today sellers were keener than buyers. Before you blame the news, ask one question: who was left to buy?
cards.simpler: Priya reads "record profits" at 9:30 am, buys at 9:40, and watches the share fall 2% by lunch. She decides the market is rigged. What really happened: the eager buyers had already bought last week, and today sellers were keener than buyers. Before you blame the news, ask one question: **who was left to buy?**

cards.prompt: Which sentence is always true about a share's price?

options.text: It rises whenever the company has a good day.
It rises when buyers want it more than owners want to sell, whatever the reason.
It shows exactly what the company is worth right now.

whyNot.a: That's the shop's day, not the crowd's: good news only lifts the price if it makes buyers keener than sellers, as Priya found.
whyNot.c: That's value, not price: price is just the last deal, and what the shop is worth can be very different.

cards.reteach: Forget the company for a second and look at the crowd at the stall. Whatever happened, the price only moves when one side, buyers or sellers, wants the deal more than the other.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A share is a tiny, real slice of owning a company, and you usually buy it from another owner, not from the company. Its price is just the last deal. Picture the jalebi stall: 40 hands up, 4 slices left, and the price climbs. Flip it, 4 hands up and 40 slices on offer, and it falls. News only matters if it changes that crowd.
cards.simpler: A share is a tiny, real slice of owning a company, and you usually buy it from another owner, not the company. Its price is just **the last deal**. Picture the jalebi stall: 40 hands up, 4 slices left, and the price climbs. Flip it, and it falls. News only matters if it changes that crowd.

cards.body:
On a weekday afternoon, search Google for a company you use, say your bank, plus "share price". Watch it for two minutes. Each change you see comes from buyers and sellers agreeing on a new price, though the number may run a little behind.

Tomorrow: why the whole country watches a list of just 30 shops.
cards.simpler:
On a weekday afternoon, search Google for a company you use, like your bank, plus "share price". Watch the number closely for two minutes. Each little jump, up or down, comes from **buyers and sellers agreeing on a new price**, though the number may run a little behind.

Tomorrow: why the whole country watches a list of just 30 shops.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain in one line why a share's price rose or fell today, using buyers and sellers instead of headlines.

dubious_claims: 'the company itself causes none of those changes' is too absolute: buybacks and the company's own announcements do move the price
'more owners wanted out than people wanted in': every trade has exactly one buyer and one seller, so the real imbalance is in who is willing to trade at the old price, not in headcount
'Every tick is one buyer and one seller agreeing': Google's share price may be delayed, and one tick can bundle many trades
Paint example: the owners holding out at ₹500 would normally fill the ₹501 and ₹502 bids first, so jumping straight to ₹503 skips how the order book actually works
repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' teach card has no concrete image, only restated ideas, and its good 'Tomorrow: 30 shops' teaser sits second-to-last, so the chapter ends on the try card instead of the hook for the next chapter.
repairedFrom.fix: Bring back the jalebi-stall crowd in card 9 ('40 hands up, 4 slices left'), then move 'Tomorrow: why the whole country watches a list of just 30 shops' so it is the very last line, after the try card.
